subject: Architecture
title: The Sydney Opera House: A Decade of Drama
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Sydney Opera House: A Decade of Drama usable.

hook.text: The Sydney Opera House was budgeted at $7 million. It cost $102 million.

buildup.text: Jørn Utzon's shell-shaped roof was so complex that no engineer knew how to build it.

discovery.text: Utzon realized every shell could be cut from a single sphere, making prefabrication possible.

twist.text: The government fired Utzon before it was finished. He never returned to see the completed building.

climax.text: The Opera House became a UNESCO World Heritage Site and Australia's most recognized symbol.

punchline.text: They fired the genius. Then put his building on every postcard.

quiz.question: How did Utzon solve the problem of building the Opera House shells?
options: He used flexible steel cables to shape each shell
He cut every shell shape from a single sphere geometry
He abandoned the original design for flat panels

details.summary: Jørn Utzon's Sydney Opera House took 16 years to build (1957-1973) — a decade over schedule and 14 times over budget. Its shell roofs were so geometrically complex that no engineering firm could build them until Utzon discovered they could all be derived from sections of a single sphere.
details.whyItMatters: The Opera House demonstrates that architectural genius and practical construction can be violently at odds. Utzon's visionary design nearly proved unbuildable.
takeaways: Took 16 years and cost 14 times the original budget
Shell roofs derived from a single sphere enabled prefabrication
Utzon resigned before completion due to political conflicts

faq.question: How did Utzon solve the shell roof problem?
faq.answer: For years, engineers couldn't determine how to build the freeform shells. Utzon's breakthrough was realizing all shells could be cut from a single sphere of the same radius.

faq.question: Why did Utzon leave the project?
faq.answer: A change in New South Wales government brought officials hostile to Utzon's design process and costs. They withheld payments and appointed a different architect for the interiors. Utzon resigned in 1966 and never returned to Australia. He received the Pritzker Prize in 2003 and died in 2008.
